hook.text: Nespresso sells coffee machines at slim margins. The real money is in the capsules: $0.80 each.

buildup.text: This is the 'razor and blade' model: cheap hardware, expensive refills you buy forever.

discovery.text: A Nespresso machine owner spends roughly $700/year on capsules—more than the machine costs.

twist.text: Third-party capsule makers erode this moat. Nespresso fights back with proprietary pod shapes.

climax.text: Consumables revenue is powerful but only works with high switching costs or lock-in.

punchline.text: The machine is the hook. Capsules pay the bills forever.

quiz.question: How does Nespresso defend its consumables model?

details.summary: Consumables revenue comes from recurring sales of products that are used up and must be repurchased. Printer ink, razor blades, coffee pods, and medical supplies generate predictable repeat purchases after the initial hardware or system is sold, often at very high margins.
details.whyItMatters: The razor-and-blade model is one of the most durable revenue strategies in business. Selling the handle cheaply locks customers into purchasing expensive proprietary consumables, creating annuity-like revenue streams with margins exceeding 60%.
takeaways: Consumables require frequent repurchasing after initial hardware purchase
Margins on consumables typically far exceed margins on the base product
Proprietary designs lock customers into branded consumable purchases

faq.question: How does the printer ink consumables model generate such high margins?
faq.answer: Printers are sold at or below cost to maximize the installed base. Replacement ink cartridges cost pennies to produce but sell for $30-60 each. DRM chips prevent third-party cartridges. Each printer generates hundreds of dollars in ink revenue over its lifetime at margins above 60%.

faq.question: How are consumables models being disrupted?
faq.answer: Third-party and generic alternatives undercut proprietary consumables. Dollar Shave Club disrupted Gillette's razor blade model with cheap subscriptions. Reusable coffee pods challenge Keurig's system. Manufacturers respond with compatibility restrictions, chip locks, and subscription plans.
